title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
You’ve probably seen the claim: insulin costs a few dollars to make, but Americans pay hundreds. Insulin was discovered more than 100 years ago, and its inventors famously sold the patent to the University of Toronto for $1 each so it would stay affordable. So how did a vial end up costing more than a car payment?
We dug into the research to see what insulin really costs to make, what other wealthy countries pay, and what the U.S. number actually means.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
The short answer






A vial of insulin (1,000 units) costs an estimated $3 to $9 to make, including a profit margin. In 2022, other wealthy countries paid an average of $24 per vial. The U.S. list price averaged $227.
But that list price is not what insurers actually paid. After secret discounts, the U.S. paid about $54, still about 2.3 times other countries. And a lot has changed since 2022.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
What it costs to make
In 2018, researchers published a detailed estimate in BMJ Global Health of what insulin would cost if many companies competed to make it, the way they do for generic pills. They added up the raw ingredients, filling and packaging the vials, building factories, getting regulatory approval, shipping, and a 20% margin for overhead and profit.



One 10 mL vial = 1,000 units. Source: Gotham, Barber & Hill, BMJ Global Health (2018).


Type of insulin
Estimated price per vial




Regular human insulin
$3.29 – $4.86


NPH (human)
$3.35 – $4.93


Glargine (Lantus-type)
$5.32 – $7.38


Lispro (Humalog-type)
$6.51 – $8.87


Aspart (Novolog-type)
$6.50 – $8.86





So yes, the viral claim holds up: insulin is cheap to make. Even the newer, longer-lasting insulins come in under $10 a vial.
What these estimates don’t include: the original research that created each insulin, the pharmacy’s markup, or insurance. They’re an estimate of what a competitive market could charge, not what any company actually spends.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
What wealthy countries pay
The RAND Corporation compared insulin prices in the U.S. and 33 other wealthy countries using 2022 sales data. These are the prices drugmakers charge before discounts, averaged across all the insulin each country uses.






The U.S. isn’t just a little higher. At $227 per vial, it was about 9.7 times the average of the other 33 countries (RAND’s careful like-for-like comparison). Canada, often the go-to comparison, was $38.
Notice something else, though: every country pays well above the cost to make it. The UK pays roughly 2 to 7 times the estimated production cost. Everyone pays a markup. The U.S. markup was just in a different league.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
section: Why the U.S. sticker price was never the real price
text:
Why the U.S. sticker price was never the real price
Here’s the part that rarely makes the viral posts. In the U.S., drugmakers set a high list price, then pay big secret rebates to the companies that manage insurance drug plans (called pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs) in exchange for being covered. RAND estimates those discounts knocked about 76% off the U.S. list price.






So who paid the $227? Often the people with the least bargaining power: the uninsured, and people in high-deductible plans, whose out-of-pocket costs are frequently based on the list price. That’s how insulin became a symbol of American health care, even though insurers were paying far less.
Researchers still argue over who’s to blame for the system. Some point to drugmakers raising list prices; others point to middlemen who earn more when list prices and rebates are both high. Either way, even after the discounts, the U.S. still paid about 2.3 times what other wealthy countries paid.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
What’s changed since 2022
The RAND data is from 2022, and the U.S. insulin market has changed a lot since then:

List price cuts. In 2023, Eli Lilly cut list prices for its main insulins by about 70%. Novo Nordisk’s cuts of 65–75% and Sanofi’s 78% cut to Lantus took effect in January 2024.
$35 caps. Since 2023, people on Medicare pay no more than $35 a month for insulin. Some states, including California, cap it for many private plans too, and the big makers offer $35 programs.
New low-cost insulin. In January 2026, California’s CalRx program and the nonprofit drugmaker Civica launched a long-acting insulin at no more than $55 for five pens, about $11 a pen. That works out to about $37 per 1,000 units, right in line with what Canada paid in 2022.

These changes don’t show up in the 2022 numbers, so today’s U.S. list prices are lower than our chart shows.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
The fine print

Different years, different sources. The cost estimate is from 2018; the country prices are from 2022.
Country prices are averages across all the insulin each country buys, so a country that uses more of the newer insulins will look a bit pricier.
U.S. discounts are estimated. Rebates are confidential, so RAND applied an average discount.
No country’s price includes the pharmacy’s markup or taxes. What patients pay at the counter can differ.

title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
text:
The bottom line
Insulin really is cheap to make, roughly $3 to $9 a vial. Other wealthy countries pay a few times that. The U.S. list price was about ten times higher than theirs, but it mostly functioned as a starting point for secret discounts, and the people who paid it were the ones least able to. After a wave of price cuts, caps, and new low-cost options since 2023, the gap is closing. But it hasn’t closed.

How we did this. Country prices are from RAND’s report Comparing Insulin Prices in the United States to Other Countries: Updated Results Using 2022 Data (Mulcahy & Schwam, 2024), which analyzed IQVIA sales data for the U.S. and 33 OECD countries (Table A.5, average gross price per 100 units, all insulins, multiplied by 10 for a 1,000-unit vial). The U.S. after-discount price applies RAND’s 76% gross-to-net estimate. Production cost estimates are from Gotham, Barber & Hill, “Production costs and potential prices for biosimilars of human insulin and insulin analogues,” BMJ Global Health (2018), Table 1. RAND report · BMJ Global Health study

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text: A night in the hospital can cost more than a used car. A routine birth can come with a bill in the thousands, even with insurance. Everyone knows American hospital care is expensive. We wanted to know how expensive, compared with what, and why.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text:
The short answer






Hospital prices have grown about 17.3× since 1980, while pay grew 4.7×. A hip replacement that private insurers paid $29,006 for in the U.S. cost $7,681 in Germany.
The biggest reasons: private insurers pay hospitals about 254% of what Medicare pays, hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies, about a quarter of hospital spending goes to administration, and hospital “list prices” are inflated far beyond cost.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
section: 45 years of hospital prices, in hours of work
text:
45 years of hospital prices, in hours of work
Like our other cost-of-living stories, we measured hospital prices against what the average worker earns. If a hospital service took 100 hours of work to pay for in 1980, here’s how many hours the same service has taken since.






Hospital care now takes about 3.7 times as many hours of work as it did in 1980. Unlike college tuition, which has started getting easier to afford, hospital prices have stayed near their peak.

The International Federation of Health Plans compared what private insurers paid for the same hospital procedures in nine countries in 2022. These are actual payments, not list prices.






Hover over any dot to see the country. The U.S. is the most expensive for every procedure. The biggest gap of all is heart bypass surgery: $89,094 in the U.S., versus $16,936 in Germany and $15,183 in Spain.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text:
Why: the four big reasons

1. Private insurance pays hospitals more than double what Medicare pays
The same hospital, the same procedure, very different prices depending on who’s paying. RAND studied claims from employer health plans across the country and found that in 2022, they paid hospitals 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same care. In some states it was over 300%.
Medicare sets its prices. Private insurers have to negotiate them, and often they don’t have much leverage, which leads to reason two.


2. Hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies
Over the past few decades, hospitals have bought each other up. KFF found that in 47% of U.S. metro areas, the entire hospital market is controlled by just one or two health systems. When an insurer has to include a hospital system in its network because there’s no alternative, that system can charge more. Research consistently finds that hospital mergers raise prices, without clear improvements in quality.


3. A quarter of the budget goes to paperwork
Billing in the U.S. is complicated: hundreds of insurers, each with its own rules, codes, and approval processes. One study found that administration took about 25% of U.S. hospital budgets, about twice the share in Canada or Scotland. (The study’s authors support a single-payer system, but the gap they measured is large under any interpretation.)


4. The “list price” is mostly fiction
Every hospital has a “chargemaster,” a master list of prices. These list prices bear little resemblance to what care costs. A study of Medicare cost data found the average hospital listed $4.32 for every $1 of its actual costs, and up to about 28 times cost for CT scans.
Medicare and insurers rarely pay list prices. The people who often get billed them are the uninsured and patients treated out of network, the ones with the least power to negotiate.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text:
The human cost
About 20 million adults owe significant medical debt (over $250), totaling at least $220 billion, according to KFF. Hospital bills are a big part of that.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text:
The fine print

Different years. Country prices and the Medicare comparison are from 2022, the administrative cost study is from 2011 data, and the list price study from 2013. The patterns have held up in later research, but the exact numbers have moved.
Country prices are medians of what private insurers paid, converted to U.S. dollars by the report’s authors. Public systems in some countries may pay less.
“Hours of work” uses the government’s hospital services price index and the average worker’s hourly pay before taxes. It tracks how prices changed, not any one bill.
What you personally pay depends on your insurance, deductible, and whether the hospital is in network.

title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
text:
The bottom line
Health economists have been saying it for decades: American health care is expensive mainly because the prices are higher, not because Americans get far more care. For hospitals, private insurers pay far more than Medicare, merged hospital systems have the leverage to keep it that way, billing complexity adds a heavy layer of cost, and inflated list prices land hardest on the people least able to pay.

How we did this. Procedure prices are from the International Federation of Health Plans and Health Care Cost Institute’s International Healthcare Cost Comparison Report 2024 (2022 data), read from the report’s charts. The Medicare comparison is from RAND’s hospital price transparency study (Round 5.1). Market concentration is from KFF. Administrative costs are from Himmelstein et al., Health Affairs (2014). List price markups are from Bai & Anderson, Health Affairs (2016). Medical debt is from KFF’s analysis of Census survey data. The hours-of-work trend uses the CPI for hospital services (BLS series CUUR0000SEMD) and average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees, both via FRED. iFHP/HCCI report · RAND · KFF on markets · KFF on medical debt

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
text:
Every time gas prices jump, someone blames the White House. Bumper stickers, memes, campaign ads: the president gets the credit when prices fall and the blame when they rise.
So we checked. We lined up every week of U.S. gas prices since April 1993 (1,753 weeks, six presidential terms) against who held the White House, the Senate, and the House.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
text:
The short answer






Adjusted for inflation, the average gallon of gas cost $3.64 under Democratic presidents and $3.64 under Republican presidents.



That tie looks suspicious, so to be clear: it’s a coincidence of averaging. Individual presidencies range from $2.55 a gallon (Bill Clinton) to $4.48 (Barack Obama), and both of those are Democrats. Each party has had cheap years and expensive years. Leave out a single presidency and the party averages split apart. What the tie does tell you is that there’s no pattern by party.
What “adjusted for inflation” means: prices rise over time, so a dollar in 1993 bought more than a dollar does now. To compare fairly, we convert every old price into today’s money. For example, the $1.07 a gallon drivers paid in 1993 bought what $2.51 buys today, so we count it as $2.51.
What actually moves the price is crude oil, and crude oil answers to wars, OPEC, recessions, and hurricanes, not to elections.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
section: 33 years of prices and who was in charge
text:
33 years of prices and who was in charge
Shading shows the president’s party (blue = Democrat, red = Republican). Gold dots are major world events. The strip underneath shows which party controlled the White House, Senate, and House. Hover for details.






The chart above is in the dollars of each week, which makes recent years look worse than they were. A dollar in 1993 bought a lot more than a dollar today, so for fair comparisons the rest of this post uses October 2026 dollars.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
text:
Finding 1: No pattern by party






We see the same thing when we look at all of Washington. Republicans in full control, Democrats in full control, or split government: the inflation-adjusted averages land within a few cents of each other. Same caution as above: each group mixes cheap years with expensive ones, so the close numbers don’t mean either party lowers prices. They mean neither one has a track record of it.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
section: Finding 2: Crude oil is the steering wheel
text:
Finding 2: Crude oil is the steering wheel
Gasoline is made from crude oil, and crude oil is priced on a world market. Here’s what gas prices would have been if you predicted them using nothing but the price of oil, against what they actually were.






The two lines barely separate. The price of crude oil alone explains 92% of the ups and downs in monthly gas prices over 33 years. As a rule of thumb, every $10 change in a barrel of oil moves a gallon of gas by about 29 cents.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
section: Finding 3: Presidents can move oil, but they don’t control it
text:
Finding 3: Presidents can move oil, but they don’t control it
Fair question: if oil drives gas prices, can’t a president drive oil prices? Sometimes, yes. The levers a president actually has:

Military action. In 2026 the U.S. and Israel struck Iran, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted, and March 2026 saw the biggest one-month jump in gas prices in this data. That one traces straight back to a decision made in the White House.
Sanctions. Limiting oil sales from countries like Iran, Venezuela, or Russia takes supply off the world market, which tends to push prices up.
The emergency oil reserve. In 2022, the White House released 180 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the largest release ever, to bring prices down.
Drilling and permits. These matter, but new wells take years to come online, so the effect usually lands on a later president’s watch.

But the biggest swings in this data came from things no president controlled:

2005: Hurricane Katrina knocked out Gulf Coast refineries.
2008: Oil hit nearly $147 a barrel, then the financial crisis crushed demand. In today’s dollars, the most expensive gas in this data was June 2008, at $6.43 a gallon.
2014–2015: OPEC kept pumping into a glut and prices collapsed.
2020: COVID lockdowns emptied the roads.
2022: Russia invaded Ukraine, and the national average hit its all-time high of $5.11 (June 2022).

So a president’s choices can push gas prices up or down, sometimes a lot. But presidents of both parties have pulled these levers, and both have been on the receiving end of world events. Over 33 years it evens out, with no party coming out ahead.

title: Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No
text:
The bottom line
Gas prices are a great way to feel the economy and a terrible way to grade a president. If you want to know where prices are headed, watch the price of oil and the news from the Middle East, not the polls.
Right now the national average is $4.29 (week of November 02, 2026). For where it’s likely headed next, see our monthly gas price tracker.

How we did this. Weekly U.S. retail gasoline prices (all grades) and weekly Brent crude prices come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Inflation adjustments use the Consumer Price Index (FRED, CPIAUCSL), converted to October 2026 dollars. Each week is assigned to whoever held the White House, Senate, and House majority that day. The “oil only” line is a simple linear regression of the monthly gas price on the monthly Brent price.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text: Electric car fans say you’ll save a fortune on gas. Skeptics say EVs cost more and lose value fast. They’re both partly right. To settle it, we compared the full cost of owning an EV, a gas car, and a hybrid of the same size and class, per year.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
The short answer






An EV saves you about $1,728 a year on fuel and maintenance (for a medium sedan). But it loses value so much faster that a new EV costs $3,080 more per year to own than a comparable gas sedan. In SUVs, it’s roughly a tie. And in every class, a hybrid was cheapest.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
How we compared them
We used AAA’s 2026 Your Driving Costs study, which averages the top-selling 2026 models in each class and adds up everything it costs to own one for five years at 15,000 miles a year:

Fuel or charging
Maintenance and repairs, including tires
Depreciation: how much value the car loses
Insurance (full coverage)
License, registration, and taxes, including the extra EV fees most states now charge
Finance charges: interest on the car loan

That puts every vehicle on the same footing: dollars per year.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
Where EVs win: running costs
The EV advantage is real. For a medium sedan, charging cost about $712 a year versus $2,215 for gas, and maintenance was cheaper too (no oil changes, fewer moving parts, and brakes that last longer thanks to regenerative braking).






One big catch: where you charge. AAA’s EV fuel costs line up with home electricity prices, which average about $0.19 per kWh nationally. Public fast chargers typically cost around $0.45 per kWh, about 2.3 times more. If you can’t charge at home and rely on fast chargers, a medium sedan’s charging bill rises to roughly $1,661 a year: still less than gas, but most of the savings are gone.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
Where EVs lose: owning costs






The biggest single cost of owning any new car is depreciation, the value it loses while you own it. For EVs, it’s brutal. AAA puts a new electric medium sedan’s depreciation at $6,786 a year, versus $3,330 for gas. Fast-improving battery technology and price cuts on new EVs make used ones worth less.
EVs also tend to cost more to insure (they’re pricier to repair), most states now charge an extra annual EV registration fee (often $100 to $250) to make up for lost gas-tax revenue, and a pricier car means more loan interest. And as of September 30, 2025, the $7,500 federal EV tax credit is gone.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
section: So who should buy an EV?
text:
So who should buy an EV?
The numbers point to a few clear cases where an EV makes financial sense:

You can charge at home. That’s where the fuel savings come from.
You drive a lot. More miles means more fuel savings to offset the extra ownership costs.
You keep cars a long time. Depreciation is heaviest in the first few years. Keep the car 10 years and the per-year cost of that early drop shrinks.
You buy used. The first owner already took the big depreciation hit. A used EV can capture the running-cost savings without paying for the steepest part of the value drop.
You’re shopping SUVs, not sedans. The gap is smallest there.

If saving money is the top priority and none of those fit, the data say: buy a hybrid. It beat both EVs and gas cars in every class AAA measured.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
The fine print

These are averages across top-selling models. A specific EV with a big discount, or a gas guzzler, can change the answer.
Five-year ownership is AAA’s assumption. Longer ownership generally helps EVs.
Electricity and gas prices vary a lot by state. Cheap power and expensive gas favor EVs.
Public charging prices vary by network and membership; ours is a typical 2026 figure.
This post is about money. Whether EVs are better for the environment is a separate question, and our follow-up post tackles it.

title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
text:
The bottom line
EVs really are cheaper to run. But “cheaper to run” isn’t “cheaper to own.” Buying new, without the old federal tax credit, an EV costs about the same as a gas SUV and more than a gas sedan, because it loses value so fast. If you can charge at home, drive a lot, keep cars for years, or buy used, the math tilts toward electric. Otherwise, a hybrid is the money winner.

How we did this. Annual costs are from AAA’s Your Driving Costs 2026 study (EV, gas, and hybrid comparison for medium sedans, compact SUVs, medium SUVs, and pickups; 15,000 miles a year, five-year ownership, full-coverage insurance). Home electricity is the BLS average U.S. price per kWh over the last 12 months, via FRED. The public fast-charging price is a typical 2026 figure from industry price trackers. title: About SixtyEight95
text: SixtyEight95 looks at everyday costs (gas, housing, groceries) using real public data. Every post shows its sources, and every projection shows how sure it is.

title: About SixtyEight95
text:
Why the name?
In statistics, the 68-95-99.7 rule says that about 68% of outcomes fall close to the average, 95% a bit further out, and 99.7% almost everywhere. It’s a reminder that a good number always comes with a range. We try to bring that same honesty to the numbers that hit your wallet.

title: About SixtyEight95
text:
Data sources
U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED, and other public datasets named in each post.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
text: If there’s one cost that defines “things were easier for our parents,” it’s college. We wanted to know how much harder it really got, and whether it’s still getting worse. So we measured it the SixtyEight95 way: in hours of work.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The short answer






Since 1980, college tuition has grown 13.8×. Hourly pay grew 4.7×, and prices for everything else grew 4.0×. So a year of college takes about 2.9 times as many hours of work as it did in 1980.
But here’s what almost nobody talks about: college peaked in 2016. Since then, pay has grown faster than tuition, and a year of college now takes about 19% fewer hours of work than at the peak.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
section: How we measure “hours of work” here
text:
How we measure “hours of work” here
For groceries and housing, we could use actual prices. For college, the government doesn’t publish one national “price of college,” because it varies so much: a community college and a private university are worlds apart. What it does publish is a price index, which tracks how much tuition and fees have changed over time for the same kinds of schools.
So we set 1980 = 100 hours and asked: if a year of college took 100 hours of work in 1980, how many hours would the same year of college take in every year since? It’s a measure of change, not a price tag, and it works for any school.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
section: 45 years of college, in hours of work
text:
45 years of college, in hours of work






From 1980 to 2016, the line almost only goes up. At the peak, a year of college took 362 hours for every 100 it took in 1980. Today it’s 293.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
section: Tuition vs. pay vs. everything else
text:
Tuition vs. pay vs. everything else






Hourly pay and general prices moved almost together for 45 years. College tuition went off on its own.
Researchers point to several reasons for the long climb, including states cutting per-student funding for public colleges (especially after the 2008 recession, which shifted more of the cost onto students), rising demand for degrees, and colleges spending more on staff and facilities.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
section: The twist: college has been getting easier to afford
text:
The twist: college has been getting easier to afford
Since 2016, tuition is up 21% while pay is up 50%. That gap is why the hours-of-work line has been falling for almost a decade.
Two things drove it:

Tuition growth slowed down. Many public universities froze or capped tuition, and enrollment has been soft, which limits how much schools can raise prices.
Pay sped up. Wages for regular workers grew quickly from 2021 to 2023, faster than they had in years.

College is still far more expensive in work time than it was in 1980. But the story of “it only ever gets worse” isn’t true anymore.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
College, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The fine print

This is a price index, not a bill. It tracks how tuition and fees changed, not what any one school charges.
Grants and scholarships vary. Many families pay less than the posted price, and how much less has changed over time.
Tuition isn’t the whole cost. Housing, food, and books are separate, and housing near campus has its own story.
Pay is the average worker’s, before taxes. It’s the same pay measure we use in every SixtyEight95 “hours of work” story, so they’re comparable.

title: College, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The bottom line
College went from expensive to very expensive between 1980 and 2016, rising far faster than paychecks. Since then, the trend has quietly reversed. A year of college still takes nearly three times the work it did in 1980, but less than it did a decade ago.

How we did this. College costs are the Consumer Price Index for “college tuition and fees” (BLS series CUUR0000SEEB01) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “Everything else” is the CPI for all items, and pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers), both via FRED. Hours of work = tuition index ÷ hourly pay, scaled so 1980 = 100. “Today” is the average of November 2025 to October 2026. BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown, so that month is skipped.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
In our last post, we found that a new EV usually isn’t cheaper to own than a gas car. So the other big argument for EVs is the environment. But you’ve probably heard the counterargument: making the batteries is so dirty that EVs aren’t really greener. Is that true?
We built a simple, transparent model from government and research data you can check, and compared it with the major lifecycle studies.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
The short answer






Building an EV’s battery creates about 4.5 tons of extra CO2 before it drives a single mile. But an EV emits so much less per mile that it pays that back after about 24,000 miles, under two years of typical driving. Over its life, a U.S. EV produces roughly half to two-thirds less CO2 than a comparable gas car.
The catch: the mining behind those batteries causes real harm, mostly far from where EVs are driven.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
The crossover
Here’s the whole story in one chart. The EV starts behind because of its battery. Then, every mile, the gas car burns gasoline while the EV draws power from the grid, which on average emits much less.






The dashed line is the break-even point: about 24,000 miles, or about 1.6 years at 15,000 miles a year. After that, every mile the EV drives puts it further ahead.

We kept this deliberately simple and, if anything, tilted toward the gas car: we count only gasoline burned in the engine, not the emissions from drilling, refining, and trucking it to the station. We also left out the rest of the car (frame, seats, glass), which takes roughly the same emissions to build either way.


How that compares with the big studies

The International Council on Clean Transportation (2021) found that a medium-size EV bought in the U.S. produces 60% to 68% less greenhouse gas over its lifetime than a comparable gas car.
The Union of Concerned Scientists (2022) found EVs produce about half the lifetime emissions, with an average break-even around 21,000 miles.
BloombergNEF estimated a typical U.S. EV breaks even after about 25,000 miles, roughly two years.

Our simple model lands right in that range: about 54% less CO2 over 150,000 miles.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
section: It depends on where you plug in
text:
It depends on where you plug in
An EV is only as clean as the power plant charging it. On the average U.S. grid, an EV emits about 107 grams of CO2 per mile. Charged entirely from coal power, that jumps to about 313 grams, slightly worse than our 30-mpg gas car’s 296.

No U.S. state runs on 100% coal, and the grid has gotten cleaner almost every year as coal plants close. The Union of Concerned Scientists found that over 90% of Americans live where driving an average EV produces less global warming pollution than even the most efficient gas car.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
The part “zero emissions” leaves out
Carbon isn’t the only kind of environmental damage. EV batteries depend on lithium, nickel, cobalt, and graphite, and getting them out of the ground has real costs:

Water. In Chile’s Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, lithium mining accounts for up to 65% of the region’s water use, according to a United Nations University report, competing with farms and local communities.
Human rights. About 70% of the world’s cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where child labor in small-scale mines has been widely documented.
Pollution where it’s processed. Nickel mining in Indonesia has been linked to deforestation and water pollution, and refining battery minerals produces far more emissions than digging them up.
Recycling is still catching up. Most of today’s EV batteries haven’t reached the end of their lives yet, and recovery of some materials, especially lithium, remains limited.

To be fair, gasoline has its own hidden costs, from oil spills to the pollution near refineries, and burning it fouls the air in the cities where people actually drive. But it’s honest to say that EVs don’t eliminate environmental damage. They shrink the climate damage a lot and move much of the remaining harm to mining regions far from the people who benefit.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
The fine print

This is a simplified model. Real results depend on the specific car, battery size, where the battery was made, how you drive, and your local grid.
Bigger batteries take longer to pay back. A large electric truck or SUV with a huge battery starts further behind than a small EV.
The grid keeps changing. Our grid figure is from 2024. A cleaner grid makes every EV mile cleaner over the car’s life.
Lifecycle studies differ in their assumptions, which is why we show several.

title: Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?
text:
The bottom line
On climate, the evidence is clear: an EV starts in the hole, climbs out in under two years of driving, and ends up responsible for roughly half to two-thirds less carbon than a gas car. The battery argument is real but much smaller than critics suggest. What “zero emissions” really hides is not carbon but where the damage happens: in the water, mines, and refineries of the places that supply the batteries.

How we did this. Gas emissions use EPA’s 8,887 grams of CO2 per gallon. Grid emissions use EIA’s 2024 U.S. average of 0.785 lb CO2 per kWh and EIA’s figure for coal-fired power. Battery manufacturing uses the ICCT’s U.S. estimate of about 60 kg CO2 per kWh. Lifecycle comparisons are from the ICCT (2021), the Union of Concerned Scientists (2022), and BloombergNEF. Mining impacts are from the United Nations University and the ICCT (2026). ICCT lifecycle study · UCS “Driving Cleaner” · EPA · EIA · ICCT on battery materials (2026)

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
Everyone has a grocery receipt that made them wince. Eggs, beef, coffee: prices really did jump after 2019. But there’s a piece missing from most of those conversations: paychecks went up too.
So instead of asking “how much does it cost?”, we asked a different question: how long do you have to work to buy it?

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
The short answer






Since 2019, average hourly pay is up 37%. That kept most groceries about as affordable as they were. The real exceptions are coffee (+67%), ground beef (+30%), and eggs (+25%), which genuinely take more of your work time than they did in 2019.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
What “minutes of work” means
We take the average price of an item and divide it by what the average worker earns per hour, before taxes. The answer is how many minutes of work it takes to pay for it.
For example, a gallon of milk costs about $4.14 today. The average worker earns about $32.25 an hour, so that gallon takes about 7.7 minutes of work. In 2019 milk was cheaper, $3.04, but pay was lower too ($23.51 an hour), so it took about 7.7 minutes. Same as now.
This works across any time period without needing to adjust for inflation, because prices and paychecks are measured in the same year’s dollars.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
2019 vs. today






Grey dot = 2019. Colored dot = today (average of November 2025 to October 2026). Hover for prices.
Prices on every item went up, by 8% to 127%. But for most of the list, pay kept pace or did better.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
section: Why coffee, beef, and eggs broke away
text:
Why coffee, beef, and eggs broke away
These three each had their own supply problem, unrelated to the general price increases since 2020:

Coffee: Bad harvests in Brazil and Vietnam, the two biggest growers, sent world coffee prices to record highs in 2024 and 2025.
Beef: Years of drought shrank the U.S. cattle herd to its smallest size in decades. Fewer cattle means pricier beef, and herds take years to rebuild.
Eggs: Bird flu outbreaks forced farms to cull millions of hens. Eggs hit their most expensive point in this data in March 2025, at 12 minutes of work for a dozen.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
section: The long view: most groceries are cheaper than in 1985
text:
The long view: most groceries are cheaper than in 1985
Here’s the part that surprises people. Of the 13 items we can track back to 1985, 12 take less work to buy today than they did then.






The exception is ground beef: 8.5 minutes of work per pound in 1985, 12.6 minutes today, near its highest level since the government started tracking it in 1984.
Farming, shipping, and stores all got more efficient over 40 years, and for most foods that kept prices rising slower than pay.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
The fine print

This is the average worker, before taxes. Your own minutes depend on your pay. If you earn less than average, every item takes longer.
These are national average prices. Your store, your city, and brand choices will differ.
Groceries aren’t the whole budget. Housing, childcare, and health care have their own stories. We’ll get to those.

title: Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work
text:
The bottom line
Grocery prices feel brutal because the dollar amounts jumped fast. Measured in time, most of the cart costs about what it did before the pandemic, and less than it did 40 years ago. The items that truly got harder to afford are coffee, beef, and eggs, each for its own reason.

How we did this. Prices are U.S. city-average retail prices from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers), also from the BLS. Both were pulled from FRED. Minutes of work = price ÷ hourly pay × 60, calculated month by month. “Today” is the average of the last 12 months of data.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
text: “Nobody can afford a house anymore” might be the most repeated money complaint in America. We wanted to know how true it is, so we measured the cost of a home the way it actually feels: in hours of work.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The short answer






The mortgage on a typical new home takes about 71 hours of work a month today. That’s a lot more than in 2021 (56 hours), but less than in 1990 (96 hours). The monthly payment isn’t the worst it’s ever been. The down payment is the bigger wall.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
What “hours of work” means
We take the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced new home and divide it by what the average worker earns per hour, before taxes. The answer is how many hours of work it takes to cover the payment each month.
For scale: a full-time job is about 173 hours a month. So today’s 71 hours is roughly 41% of one person’s pay before taxes. (Many households have two earners, which makes it easier, but we stick to one so the comparison is the same in every year.)

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
section: 50 years of mortgage payments, in hours
text:
50 years of mortgage payments, in hours






Hover to see the price, the rate, and the payment behind each point.
The worst moment was the end of 1981, when mortgage rates were near 18% and the payment took 124 hours a month. The best was 2011, at 49 hours, with rates around 4%.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
section: Interest rates are the big lever
text:
Interest rates are the big lever
Notice what happened between 2021 and 2023. Home prices relative to pay barely moved, but the payment went from 56 hours to 87 hours of work a month. That jump was almost all interest rates, which went from about 3% to 6.8%.
To see how much rates matter: today’s median new home costs about $406,900. At today’s rate (about 6.4%), the monthly payment is about $2,280. At 2021’s rate, the same house would cost $1,536 a month. Same house, $744 a month difference.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
section: The catch: getting in the door
text:
The catch: getting in the door
The monthly payment is only half the story. Before you get a mortgage, you need a down payment, and that depends on the price of the house, not the interest rate.






A 10% down payment on a typical new home is about $40,690 today. That’s 7.3 months of the average worker’s full pay, before taxes and before spending a dime on anything else. In 1985 it was 5.6 months.
That’s why buying feels so out of reach even though the monthly payment isn’t at a record: the house itself costs more years of pay than it did in the 1980s, so the savings hurdle is higher.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The fine print

Principal and interest only. Property taxes and homeowners insurance aren’t included, and insurance in particular has gotten much more expensive in many states. Real monthly costs are higher than shown.
Newly built homes. The government’s long-running median price series covers new homes. Existing homes follow a similar trend, but prices differ.
National medians. A typical home in San Francisco and one in Toledo are very different stories.
One average earner, before taxes. Your own hours depend on your pay and your household.

title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
text:
The bottom line
Monthly mortgage payments are high compared with the cheap-money years of 2010–2021, but not compared with the 1980s and early ’90s. What’s genuinely harder now is the price of entry: the down payment takes more of a paycheck than it did a generation ago. If rates come down, the monthly payment gets easier fast. The down payment problem only gets easier if pay grows faster than home prices.

How we did this. Home prices are the median sales price of new houses sold in the U.S. (Census Bureau and HUD). Mortgage rates are Freddie Mac’s 30-year fixed average. Pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. All series come from FRED. We assume 10% down and a 30-year fixed loan at that quarter’s average rate. Hours of work = monthly payment ÷ hourly pay. “Today” is the average of the latest four quarters (through Q3 2026).
